messages.subject: new ASM book: volunteer proof readers sought
messages.subject_clean: new ASM book: volunteer proof readers sought
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Ken Kellner and I have written a new book on applied statistical modeling, which will be published by Elsevier in 2024: Applied Statistical Modeling for Ecologists.

The new 'ASM book' is the successor of the widely used textbook Introduction to WinBUGS for Ecologists and covers applied parametric statistical modeling using linear, generalized linear, generalized linear mixed, hierarchical and integrated models, using likelihood alongside Bayesian inference. We fit every model using JAGS, NIMBLE and Stan, as well as using 'canned' functions in R and TMB. Thus, our new book can be used equally well as an intro to the topic of its title, as well as a quick-start guide for any of JAGS, NIMBLE, Stan, and TMB. We give a lot of coverage to the foundational method of maximum likelihood, which we apply to all models using our own functions, and in addition we have a long chapter on the important topics of model checking and model selection.

Now, we are looking for people who would volunteer to help reading chapter proofs, which are due in mid-February. If you'd be interested to proof-read one or more chapters, then please send Ken an email at kell...@msu.edu, with CC to marc...@hotmail.com. Your job would be to read and return within at most 7 days the chapter(s) of your choice and mark up any errors in either text or code.

In the attached flyer, you find more information about the book content and a list of all the chapters with their approximate length. Please feel free to send to other people who might be interested in this.

Thank you very much !

Best regards

Marc + Ken

messages.subject_clean: Fixed bug in occu() when using the TMB engine
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The occu() function in the released version of unmarked on CRAN can give incorrect answers under specific circumstances. If *all* of the following apply to your analysis:

1. Used occu()
2. Fit a random effect (or used engine = "TMB")
3. Had detection covariate(s)
4. Had a large number of missing values in the encounter history
5. The missing values were interspersed among non-missing observations (rather than just used to pad out the end of each encounter history to handle unbalanced designs)

then the resulting estimates of the slopes in the detection model may be incorrect. I've pushed a fix to the dev version which you can install with the following code:

remotes::install_github("rbchan/unmarked")

I'll submit a new version to CRAN on January 8 when they open back up after the holiday. Thanks to Marc Kery for identifying this problem, and sorry for any problems it has caused.

Ken

messages.subject_clean: New unmarked release 1.4.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

There is a new version of unmarked on CRAN (1.4.1). The windows binary package is not available yet but should be in the next couple days.

This version fixes the bug in occu() with random effects I described a few days ago (https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/e2oiLcQemn8).

It also adds support for two new models:

* goccu(), which fits detection/non-detection data with two scales (temporal or spatial) collected in a robust-design-like framework (see  ?goccu and DOI:0.1111/j.1365-2664.2008.01509.x for an example). This allows estimation of an availability parameter.

* occuCOP(), which fits a single-season occupancy model using count data (see ?occuCOP and DOI:10.1101/2023.11.17.567350).

Many thanks to Léa Pautrel for contributing occuCOP to unmarked! Let us know if you run into problems with either new function.

Ken

I browsed through old posts and couldn't find an answer to this, but apologies if I missed a similar question...

I'm fitting an occuMulti model with two species, and I have interest explicitly in determining (1) if these species occur independently AND (2) if and how co-occurrence changes across a latitudinal gradient. I'm not interested in trying to infer interactions between species, per se...just in co-occurrence between the two species (likely due in part to use of similar habitat), so I've been purposefully sparse on habitat covariates for the first-order natural parameters. I'm addressing this question by running one model where the form of the occupancy model is:

 '~lat_st + elev_st + elev_st_sq',
 '~lat_st + elev_st + elev_st_sq',
 '~lat_st'

where lat_st is standardized latitude, and elev_st and elev_st_sq are standardized elevation and its quadratic form. To draw inference about independence of species occurrence, I'm interpreting the intercept and the latitude coefficient for f12 (i.e., for simplicity, just looking at 95% CI overlap with zero). The thing is, rather than just predicting how co-occurrence changes across the latitudinal gradient with predict(umf.fit, 'state', species=c(1,2), newdata = PredDat), I'm also interested in looking at how f12 itself (and its significance) changes over the latitudinal gradient. Calculating f12 at different latitudinal gradients is simple using the f12 sub-model (f12 = intercept + slope*lat_st), but I'm interested in calculating confidence intervals, as well, and I've gotten a little stuck with how to correctly propagate the error...happy to use delta method or bootstrapping, but I'm stuck on the details of how to do either!

Any tips would be greatly appreciated! Thanks in advance!

Kristin

Dear Ken (and ALL)

I'm using ubms for pcount models. I start simply and build up their complexity. I have had success with the following six models on a dataset previously. However, for my most recent dataset one model (mod_cov_1) just will not complete the cycle and is stuck at the end of chain 4 processing.

I have tried different computers, one with higher memory. All the other models run well (40 mins - 2hr 30). I left mod_cov_1 running overnight as I considered I may not have been patient enough. No change. I am using the latest R Studio and R (4.3.2).

Any advice welcome. Many thanks. This is an excellent group forum.

Todd Lewis - UWE Bristol

(mod_null_0 <- stan_pcount(~1 ~1,
                          K=20, chains=4, iter=2000,
                          UMF, seed=2023, cores=6)) #iter2000 final

(mod_null_1 <- stan_pcount(~scale(Depth) ~1,
                          K=20, chains=4, iter=2000,
                          UMF, seed=2023, cores=6))

(mod_cov_1 <- stan_pcount(~1 ~Location,

Dear all,

I am trying to determine the effects of factors related to stream drying and permanence on colonization and extinction dynamics of a crayfish species, and I am using the unmarkedMultFrame function in unmarked to get at this question. I collected presence/absence data at 23 sites for 4 seasons (summer 1, fall 1, summer 2, fall 2) which are my primary periods, and I have 2 secondary sampling surveys for each season.

I am having issues with the null model estimate for extinction probability. The estimate I get for null extinction is 0.0925. Since this is not an estimate that I typically see (e.g. ~ 0.100 - 0.999), I am wondering if there is something wrong, or if the null extinction estimate for this species is in fact 0.0925.
